A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Chart2Code and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. Content can be matched across extensive reformatting and renumbering. Internal reporting inconsistencies limit some interpretations but do not prevent comparison.

before.justification: Tables 3–5 and Appendix D report original model evaluations measuring execution rates and code/chart quality across the three benchmark levels.

after.justification: The revised model evaluations report original empirical results, and Appendix F adds a human study assessing agreement with automated scores.

M1.justification: The generation procedure and Figure-object base evaluators are retained. The proposed judging component changes from six LLM dimensions to eight with joint structured output, revised aggregation, and new image-judge scoring rules in Appendix M.

E1.justification: The three tasks, data domains, and 22 overall chart types remain. Figure 2 newly lists radar under Level 3 and omits bar under Level 2, but the prose retains the earlier 19/12 family counts. This inconsistency prevents confidently distinguishing actual coverage changes from distribution-reporting errors; increased sample counts alone do not establish broader coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 3–5 replace GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5-Pro with GPT-5.2 and Gemini-3-Pro. Tables 3–4 add reported comparisons involving GLM-4.6V-Flash, Qwen3-VL-32B, and InternVL-3.5-38B. The existing Qwen3-VL-30B variants correspond to the later 30B-A3B naming.

E3.justification: Judging changes from six weighted LLM dimensions to eight, with explicit image-score caps and failure rules. Level 3 expands from 150 tasks using 39 Excel files to 313 tasks using 71 files. Appendix F introduces a human-validation protocol with 20 raters, seven models, and task-specific sampling.

E4.justification: Appendices E–F add code/chart metric correlations, three detailed Claude-Sonnet-4 scoring cases, and direct validation against human ratings. These examine evaluator validity and failure mechanisms beyond v1's analyses. The existing difficulty breakdown, ten-case heatmaps, and user-centric examples are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: The new validation reports Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall agreement, RMSE, and bias, with shaded regression bands in Figure 18. These statistical reporting practices were absent from v1. Band construction and confidence levels are unspecified, and benchmark repeated-run uncertainty remains unreported.

E6.justification: Tables 3–5 contain extensive numerical revisions beyond score rescaling: Claude-Sonnet-4's editing LMM-score changes from 0.2147 to 25.40 on the later 100-point scale. Weighted Base scores, dimension-level LLM results, and human-agreement results are added. Revised judging and experimental settings preclude interpreting these as same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: The aggregate score definition changes from six weighted LLM components to eight, with data and color weighted 0.2 each and the remaining dimensions 0.1; v2 also defines this aggregation for Base-Score. The existing Figure-based matching definitions and derivations remain substantially equivalent, with no new theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The hierarchical benchmark contribution and central claim that visual fidelity lags executability remain. The introduction strengthens the positioning claim by explicitly declaring ChartMimic insufficiently challenging or discriminative for current and future models, beyond v1's benchmark-versus-real-world mismatch argument.

C2.justification: V1's speculative evaluator-anomaly discussion gives way to measured human-agreement, weak CRD correlation, and upward-bias interpretations. Appendix E.2 adds mechanisms linking code reasoning to visual fidelity and expanded limitations. Its description of code scores as reliable visual proxies conflicts with the main text's poor-correlation interpretation.

D1.justification: Appendix D.4 and Table 6 add annotator workloads, recruitment, compensation, consent, and guidance details. Model configuration/source tables add checkpoints for newer models, and data-source documentation expands. The extensive base-evaluator code listings and the code/data access destination are retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for Qwen3-VL, Gemini 3, GPT-5.2, and Zhipu's newer model. It elaborates the distinction between analytical editing and ChartEdit's localized edits. The established related-work coverage and benchmark comparison set largely remain.

P1.justification: The introduction, task explanations, and evaluation narrative undergo substantial rewriting. Related work and data curation move into appendices, task definitions gain a separate hierarchy section, and limitations and conclusion become separate sections. The judging prompts are extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout throughout. Result tables gain aggregate and dimension-level displays, and new correlation plots, scoring-case tables, and a human-evaluation interface are added. Existing heatmaps, performance charts, examples, and code listings are extensively relocated or reformatted.

improvement.justification: Human calibration and annotation disclosures address important gaps in v1. However, v2's Figures 22 and 24 retain v1 results under updated model names while conflicting with its tables, and its abstract attributes Gemini's Table 4 scores to GPT-5.2. Appendix M also caps any error at 40 while allowing 70–89 for minor differences. These unresolved issues affect the central evaluation, preventing a reliable net judgment between improved validation and reduced reporting consistency.
